title: Senior's toolkit: the first five minutes with a dataset
summary: info, describe, value_counts, sample and display options: what analysts run on every new table before they trust it.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: the first five minutes with a dataset
steps.body: Before any chart or model, experienced analysts profile the data: types, missing values, ranges, odd categories. Five calls catch most of the surprises that would otherwise reach a stakeholder.

toolkit.what: Rows, columns, each column's dtype and non-null count, and the real memory used. A text column (`object` or `str`) where you expected numbers is the first red flag.
flags: count the real size of strings, not just pointers
always show non-null counts, even for wide frames

toolkit.what: Count, mean, spread, min and max for numbers; count, unique and top value for text. Impossible values (negative ages, a max of 99999) show up here.
flags: text and category columns too, not only numbers
look at the tails, where the bad rows live
transpose, so each column is a row: easier to read

toolkit.what: How often each value appears. Without `dropna=False`, missing values silently vanish from the counts.
flags: count NaN as its own row

toolkit.what: Distinct values per column. Tells you which columns are ids (unique per row), categories (few values) or constants (one value: useless).
Random rows, not just the first five. `head()` shows how the file starts, which is often the cleanest part.
flags: a number of rows or a fraction
the same rows every run, so you can share what you saw

toolkit.what: Stop pandas hiding columns behind `...` when you inspect a wide table.
flags: how many columns to show (None: all)

toolkit.cmd: Shift+Enter, Esc A / B, Esc M
toolkit.what: Jupyter and VS Code notebook keys. Add `?` after any name to read its docs in the notebook.
flags: run the cell and move to the next
turn the cell into Markdown notes

steps.prompt: The table has 1,000 orders. `df["country"].value_counts()` shows UK 480, US 300, FR 20, which adds up to 800. What happened to the other 200?
options: They have no country (NaN), and `value_counts` drops NaN by default; use `value_counts(dropna=False)`
`value_counts` only shows countries with at least 20 rows
The other 200 rows are duplicates and were removed
steps.explain: Missing values are excluded unless you ask for them. A fifth of the data having no country is a finding to report, not a detail to lose.

steps.prompt: `df.info()` lists `amount` with a text dtype (`object`, or `str` in pandas 3). You expected a number. What does that tell you?
options: At least one value is not a clean number (for example `"£12.50"` or `"n/a"`), so pandas kept the column as text; sums and means will be wrong or fail
pandas always stores money as text
The column is fine; text columns sum the same way as numbers
The file is corrupted and must be downloaded again
steps.explain: One bad value makes the whole column text. Find the offenders before converting: the cleaning module shows `pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")` and how to list what it could not parse.

steps.prompt: Match each argument to what it does.
pairs: measure the real size of text columns
describe text columns as well as numbers
the same random rows on every run

steps.prompt: Which call answers the question fastest?
items: Which columns have missing values, and what type is each?
How much memory does this table use?
What are typical and extreme order totals?
How many orders per payment method, including blanks?
What share of users are on each plan?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Run `info`, `describe`, `value_counts(dropna=False)` on the key columns and a random `sample` on every new dataset, and write down what surprised you. Most wrong numbers in reports trace back to a check someone skipped in these five minutes.
